docs.title: Physics Graduate Council Wiki
docs.text:
Shared reference material for the Physics graduate community at UC San Diego. This is a reference repository, not a news feed — pages here are meant to stay useful for years, and to be corrected when they drift.

docs.title: What belongs here
docs.text:
Reference information that more than one person needs and that nobody wants to re-derive every year: deadlines, procedures, "who do I email about X", the unwritten norms of the department.

What does not belong here: member contact lists, financial records, or anything else you would not want publicly readable. This repository is public — see About for why.

Anyone can fix a page

See something wrong or out of date? Click the pencil icon at the top right of any page. It opens GitHub's web editor — no software to install. See MAINTAINING.md for the full workflow.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
This repository is public, and has to be — GitHub's free plan only serves Pages from public repos. Everything committed here is world-readable and stays in the git history forever, even after deletion.

Never commit

  • Member contact lists or rosters
  • Financial records, budgets tied to named people
  • Anything shared with you in confidence
  • Credentials of any kind

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Corrections are welcome from anyone. Click the pencil icon at the top right of any page to edit it in the browser, or open a pull request if you prefer. A maintainer reviews and merges; the site rebuilds automatically.

docs.title: Coursework
docs.text:
What you have to take, in what order, and to what standard.

Requirements change — check the department site

This section reflects the department's orientation handbook. The Physics department website and the UCSD catalog are authoritative if they disagree.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
• 7 core courses, grade of B or better.
  • 2 electives, grade of B+ or better.
  • 5 advanced graduate courses from at least 3 different groups, grade of C or better, with a 3.0 average across four of the five — by the end of your third year.
  • At least one quarter of TAing.
  • Maintain a 3.0 GPA overall and a satisfactory annual evaluation.

Core courses and electives are expected by the end of your first year, but you have up to two years. Students who have not qualified after two years may be asked to leave the program. Biophysics students get an extra year at each stage.

docs.title: The first-year sequence
docs.text:
Fall Winter Spring 200A Theoretical Mechanics 203A Adv. Classical Electrodynamics I 203B Adv. Classical Electrodynamics II 201 Mathematical Physics 212B Quantum Mechanics II 210A Equilibrium Statistical Mechanics 212A Quantum Mechanics I Elective I Elective II 500 Intro to Physics Teaching

36 units total. PHYS 500 is mandatory and fall-only for first-years.

Depending on your diagnostic exam results, you may be directed into upper-division undergraduate courses instead to close gaps first.

docs.title: Registration basics
docs.text: Every full-time graduate student registers for at least 12 units per quarter. Beyond the core courses, students top up with colloquium (PHYS 260), research seminars, and research units (PHYS 298 before candidacy, PHYS 299 after). See Enrollment for the mechanics.

docs.title: Academic standing
docs.text:
A 3.0 GPA and a satisfactory annual departmental evaluation are both required. The evaluation goes to the Dean of the Graduate Division (GEPA) and determines whether you continue in the program and whether your financial support continues. See Annual Evaluation.

A departmental Qualification Committee reviews every student's first-year coursework over the summer and recommends corrective measures for anyone below the grade standards.

docs.title: Course notes
docs.text:
The most useful thing this section could hold that no official document provides: honest, student-written notes on what each course is actually like — workload, grading, whether the textbook matters, what to review beforehand.

Add a page per course when there is enough to say. A file named phys-200a.md in this folder appears under Coursework automatically.

docs.title: Advanced Graduate Courses
docs.text:
You need five of these, from at least three different groups, with a grade of C or better and a 3.0 average across four of the five, completed no later than the end of your third year.

Electives taken to satisfy the core requirement may also count here.

Alternative route

Instead of the course requirement, you may petition to take an oral examination covering three areas of physics.

docs.text: Biophysics PhD students select five courses from Biology, Biochemistry, Chemistry, or Physics, chosen in consultation with their adviser. At least three must be graduate courses, and any Physics courses come from the eight groups above.

docs.text: The department distributes a printable checklist covering the first-year grid and every advanced course above, with a box per course, plus checkboxes for PHYS 500 and the one-quarter TA requirement. docs.title: Academic Deadlines
docs.text:
All academic deadlines are set by the Office of the Registrar and are subject to change. The ones below are specific to graduate students and identical in all three quarters — which makes them worth memorizing once.

Count Fridays, not dates

These deadlines are defined by week of the quarter, not calendar date, so they hold from year to year. For the actual dates in a given term, see the Registrar's Enrollment and Registration Calendar.

docs.title: The recurring pattern
docs.text:
Deadline What is due 2nd Friday Half-time study requests · Leave of absence · In absentia requests · Applications to candidacy for the Master's degree (all via the GEPA tool) 4th Friday Add/drop/change via EASy — change a grading option, change units, or drop a course without a W 9th Friday Drop a course via EASy 10th Friday Add a course via EASy 11th Friday (finals week) Final paperwork for degree completion

Department approval is not the deadline

Fully completed forms must be received by GEPA by the deadline. Departmental approval alone does not count as meeting it.

To receive the Master's in the same quarter you apply, the candidacy application must land by the 2nd Friday.

docs.title: Degree completion
docs.text:
Spring degree. To have your name printed in the commencement booklet, all final paperwork is due the Friday of 10th week. The absolute final deadline is the last Friday of spring quarter, but a submission that late will not get your name in the booklet.

Summer degree. The last Friday of summer session II — usually early September.

docs.title: Shape of the academic year
docs.text:
Exact dates change annually, but the rhythm does not:

Quarter Instruction begins Instruction ends Fall Late September Early December, finals following Winter Early January Mid-March, finals following Spring Late March Early-to-mid June, finals following

Each quarter runs roughly 48–49 days of instruction. Commencement follows the end of spring quarter.

Holidays observed during the academic year include Veterans Day, Thanksgiving, winter break and New Year, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents' Day, Cesar Chavez Day, and Memorial Day.

For the authoritative version, see the UCSD academic calendar.

docs.title: Enrollment deadline for incoming students
docs.text: Separate from the above, and the one that catches new students: the deadline to enroll and pay fees falls before instruction begins in fall. Missing it costs $100 in late fees. See Enrollment.

docs.title: PhD Requirements
docs.text:
The full path from arrival to defense.

Check the department site for updates

These requirements come from the department's orientation handbook. The Physics department website is authoritative.

docs.title: Diagnostic exam
docs.text:
Entering students take an entrance diagnostic exam on undergraduate physics, covering:

  • Mechanics
  • Electricity and magnetism
  • Quantum mechanics
  • Statistical mechanics
  • Mathematical methods

It is not pass/fail in the usual sense — it is placement. Students found to have serious gaps are directed into appropriate upper-division undergraduate courses. Your graduate advisor meets with you once results are available, and that meeting shapes your first-year schedule.

docs.title: Core courses and electives
docs.text:
Seven core courses, each with a grade of B or better:

Course Title PHYS 200A Theoretical Mechanics I PHYS 201 Mathematical Methods in Physics PHYS 203A Advanced Classical Electrodynamics I PHYS 203B Advanced Classical Electrodynamics II PHYS 210A Equilibrium Statistical Mechanics PHYS 212A Quantum Mechanics I PHYS 212B Quantum Mechanics II

Plus two elective courses with a grade of B+ or better. Electives may also count toward the advanced graduate course requirement below — the same course can satisfy both.

Timing. Expected by the end of the first year, with up to two years allowed. A departmental Qualification Committee reviews all students and recommends corrective measures for those below standard. Students who have not qualified after two years may be asked to leave the program.

Biophysics students are expected to finish by the end of their second year, with an additional year if needed.

docs.title: Advanced graduate courses
docs.text:
Five advanced courses, grade of C or better, from at least three of the eight groups, with a 3.0 average across four of the five. Due no later than the end of the third year.

In lieu of the course requirement, students may petition to take an oral examination covering three areas of physics instead.

The full group listings are on Advanced Graduate Courses.

docs.title: Teaching requirement
docs.text:
Every graduate student must participate in the undergraduate teaching program. The core of it is at least one quarter of Teaching Assistantship, in either a lecture or a laboratory course, and the main component is an evaluated classroom-based teaching activity. All teaching accomplishments are subject to approval by the Vice Chair for Education.

Several routes satisfy it:

  1. Leading discussions as a Teaching Assistant
  2. Working as a Lab TA
  3. Practical classroom teaching under faculty supervision
  4. An approved teaching development program, from the department or the campus Center for Teaching Development
  5. Transferred teaching credit from another institution or department

Students satisfying it by teaching at UCSD enroll in PHYS 500 in the fall quarter of their first year. See Teaching.

docs.title: Qualifying exam and advancement to candidacy
docs.text:
To advance, you must have met the departmental requirements and secured a faculty research supervisor.

When you apply to advance, the Dean of Graduate Studies and Research appoints a doctoral committee that oversees the rest of your program. That committee conducts the qualifying examination, in which you must demonstrate the ability to engage in thesis research — usually by presenting a plan for your thesis project. The committee may ask about the project directly or indirectly, plus general physics it considers relevant.

Passing advances you to candidacy and earns you the C.Phil. degree.

Target: advance by the end of your third year.

docs.title: Thesis defense
docs.text: Once the thesis is complete, you present and defend it before your doctoral committee.

docs.title: Annual evaluation
docs.text: Separately from all of the above, every student is evaluated annually and must submit a written progress report by June 30. Continued financial support depends on it. See Annual Evaluation.

docs.title: Timeline at a glance
docs.text:
Year Milestone First Core courses and electives; diagnostic exam; PHYS 500; begin research over summer Second Finish core and electives; start advanced courses; secure a research advisor by end of spring Third Research; finish course requirements; advance to candidacy Fourth+ Research, write, defend

See Quarter-by-Quarter Timeline for the detailed first year.

docs.title: First-Year Onboarding
docs.text:
Everything a new Physics graduate student needs before and during their first few quarters. If you have just accepted an offer, start here.

The short version

  1. Set up your PID and password, then enroll in classes before the deadline — see Enrollment.
  2. Submit your ID card photo online before you arrive.
  3. Show up to both days of department orientation in mid-September. They are mandatory.
  4. Sign up for direct deposit immediately — see Pay and Payroll.
  5. Take the diagnostic exam; your advisor meeting follows from it.

docs.title: Before you arrive
docs.text:
• Log in to your application and set up your PID and password. You need these for WebReg, TritonLink, and everything else.
  • Enroll in fall classes. Do not wait for orientation — see Enrollment for the required courses and the deadline.
  • Submit your photo through the Online Photo Tool so your Triton ID is ready. The department collects IDs and hands them out at orientation.
  • Keep your mailing address current on TritonLink. Paychecks and official mail follow it.
  • Arrange housing — apply early, the queue is long. See Housing.
  • Gather your employment documents (I-9 identity and work-eligibility documents). See Employment Paperwork.
  • International students: check whether you need the ELCE before you can TA — see English Certification for International TAs.

docs.text:
What When Details English Language Certification Exam Late August to mid-September International students only — ELCE Department orientation, Day 1 and Day 2 Two consecutive days, mid-September Mandatory — Orientation Diagnostic exam Before instruction begins Diagnostic Exam Meeting with your graduate advisor September, after diagnostic results Advisors contact you to schedule Lab TA training Roughly the day before instruction begins For Physics 1-series lab TAs Instruction begins Late September Academic Deadlines

Exact dates shift every year. The department emails a final orientation schedule in early September — that email is authoritative, not this page.

docs.title: Where things are
docs.text: Office space First-year TAs share assigned office space in Mayer Hall Addition rooms 5702 and 5712, with tables and lockers. Your ID card is coded for Mayer Hall, those two rooms, and the Graduate Student Lounge (MHA 5205). Lab TAs and lab coordinators also get lab access. Mailboxes Third floor, Mayer Hall Addition room 3623. University and departmental mail only — send personal mail to your home address. Check it weekly. Wifi and IT Campus wireless setup is on Blink. See Campus Services. Printing Departmental copiers are for official use only, not class notes or personal printing. Use the University Libraries for personal copying. GSRs who need to duplicate research material should ask their supervisor about using the group's budget number.

docs.title: Enrollment
docs.text:
How to register for classes as an incoming student, and the deadlines attached.

Enroll before you arrive

The enrollment deadline falls before instruction begins, not after. Missing it costs $100 in late fees ($50 for late enrollment plus $50 for late payment of fees). You can enroll as soon as your PID and password are set up — do not wait for orientation.

docs.title: Required fall courses
docs.text:
All first-year students enroll in these:

Course Title Units PHYS 200A Theoretical Mechanics 4 PHYS 201 Mathematical Physics 4 PHYS 212A Quantum Mechanics 4 PHYS 500 Introduction to Physics Teaching 1 (mandatory)

PHYS 500 is mandatory for all first-year students and is only offered in fall. It prepares you for the teaching requirement every graduate student has to satisfy — see Teaching.

If your diagnostic exam results suggest gaps, your advisor may direct you into upper-division undergraduate courses instead of, or alongside, part of this list.

docs.title: The 12-unit minimum
docs.text:
All full-time graduate students — including TAs, GSRs, and fellows — must register for at least 12 units every quarter. The three core courses give you 12 on their own, but most students pad the total with:

  • PHYS 260 (Colloquium) — 0 or 1 unit. Thursdays at 4:00 p.m. Everyone is expected to attend.
  • Research seminars in your area (for example PHYS 251, High Energy Seminar) — 0 or 1 unit each, if you plan to attend regularly.
  • PHYS 261 (Physics Research at UC San Diego) — 0 or 1 unit, winter quarter only. A weekly series introducing the department's research groups and faculty. Scheduled not to conflict with graduate courses.
  • PHYS 298 (research, before advancing to candidacy) or PHYS 299 (after advancing) — one or more units, S/U graded.

Seminars and colloquium are graded S (satisfactory) only, and require attendance rather than coursework.

docs.title: How to enroll
docs.text:
1. Go to TritonLink.
  2. Under Classes & Enrollment, choose WebReg. Sign in with your student Single Sign-On.
  3. Choose the term and submit.
  4. Add classes either by typing the section ID directly, or through the advanced search — enter the subject and set student level to Graduate. Click the blue underlined section number, then Enroll.

The course catalog lists every Physics course and its description.

docs.title: Tuition and fees
docs.text:
If you were awarded a tuition and fee scholarship, enroll first — the department processes your fee payment once you are enrolled. Scholarship students see the payment appear as a credit on their fee statement via electronic transmission.

Students supported as TAs, graders, or GSRs at 25% time or more in a given quarter have tuition, fees, and health insurance paid for that quarter as a benefit of employment.

Full detail, including what you pay if you are unsupported, is in Funding and Fees.

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text:
The department runs a two-day orientation in mid-September, in the week before instruction begins. Both days are mandatory.

The emailed schedule wins

Exact dates, times, and rooms change every year. The department emails a final orientation schedule in early September — that is the authoritative version. This page describes the shape of the week so you know what to expect and what to prepare.

docs.text:
When What Notes Late August to mid-September English Language Certification Exam (ELCE) International students only — see ELCE September, after diagnostic results Meeting with your graduate advisor Advisors reach out to schedule; results drive the conversation Mid-September, full day (roughly 8:30 a.m.–3:00 p.m.) Department Orientation, Day 1 Mandatory The next day, full day Department Orientation, Day 2 Mandatory Roughly the day before instruction Lab TA training, Physics 1-series Led by the Physics 1-series lab instructors Late September Instruction begins

Orientation has recently been held in Mayer Hall Addition 2722.

docs.title: Research
docs.text:
Finding a group, the deadlines attached to that, and the mechanics of doing research here.

The deadline that matters

You must secure a research advisor by the end of spring quarter of your second year. Everything else on this page works backward from that.

docs.title: Finding a group
docs.text:
The department front-loads the introductions:

  • PHYS 261 — Physics Research at UC San Diego runs weekly in winter quarter, specifically to introduce you to the department's research and the faculty doing it. It is scheduled not to conflict with graduate courses. Register for 0 or 1 unit. This is the single most efficient way to survey the department.
  • PHYS 260 — Colloquium, Thursdays at 4:00 p.m., all year.
  • Area seminars (for example PHYS 251, High Energy Seminar) — register for 0 or 1 unit if you will attend regularly.
  • Tea time, weekly during the academic year, is the informal version. See Student Life.

Start research in the summer after your first year. That is the expected point, and summer research assistantships are often available then, subject to federal funding. Arrange these directly with the professor running the project.

What is it like to work with them?

Advisor Reviews collects students' own accounts of working with particular faculty — group size, meeting cadence, funding stability, advising style. It is the information you cannot get from a seminar. Read the ground rules there before submitting one yourself.

docs.title: Funding follows the advisor
docs.text:
After the first year, students are encouraged to affiliate with a research group and be supported as a Graduate Student Researcher (GSR) rather than a TA. Ask the faculty member you want to work with about support well in advance — spring quarter for the following year.

GSR funding comes from federal contracts and grants, so appointments depend on funds being available that year. Some TA positions remain available to advanced students, and fellowship holders can often hold a partial TA or GSR appointment alongside. See Funding and Fees.

docs.title: Registering for research units
docs.text:
Course Who PHYS 298 Students not yet advanced to candidacy PHYS 299 Students advanced to candidacy

Both are S/U graded. Research units are how most students reach the 12-unit minimum once coursework thins out.

docs.title: Advancing to candidacy
docs.text:
To advance you need the departmental requirements met and a faculty research supervisor. A doctoral committee is appointed, conducts your qualifying examination — usually a presentation of your thesis research plan — and on success you advance and receive the C.Phil. degree.

Target: advance by the end of your third year. Full detail in PhD Requirements.

docs.title: Year-by-year
docs.text: Year What is expected First Coursework. Begin research over the summer; the Qualification Committee reviews your first-year grades. Second Finish core courses and electives. Begin advanced courses. Secure a research advisor by end of spring. Third Research. Finish course requirements. Advance to candidacy. Fourth+ Research, write the thesis, defend before your PhD committee.

docs.title: Every year, regardless
docs.text: A written progress report is due to your advisor by June 30, and the department submits an evaluation of you to GEPA each spring. Continued funding depends on it — see Annual Evaluation.

docs.title: Practical matters
docs.text: Conference travel Replace this with how reimbursement actually works, who approves it, and how far ahead to book. Note that direct deposit for Disbursements (travel and personal reimbursement) is set up separately from payroll — see Pay and Payroll. Computing Replace with cluster access, storage, and software licenses. Duplicating research material Departmental copiers are for official use. GSRs needing to duplicate research material should ask their supervisor or group administrator about using the group's budget number.

docs.title: Annual Evaluation
docs.text:
Every graduate student is evaluated once a year on progress toward candidacy and thesis defense. Continued financial support depends on it.

June 30

Your written progress report is due to your advisor by June 30 every year. It is short — no more than two typed pages — but it is not optional.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text: The University and the department both require an annual evaluation of each student's progress. It matters especially if your research advisor is not a member of the Physics department, since nobody else is tracking you. The stated purpose is to identify and correct problems early enough to keep your PhD on schedule.

docs.title: What the department does
docs.text:
Each spring quarter, the department submits an annual evaluation on every graduate student to GEPA (the Division of Graduate Education and Postdoctoral Affairs), covering progress toward candidacy and defense.

Continued support is contingent on GEPA receiving that report by the end of spring quarter.

Separately, during spring quarter the department gives every student a written evaluation of performance in coursework, research, and teaching. That evaluation goes to the Dean of the Graduate Division and forms the basis for deciding whether you continue in the program and whether your funding continues.

docs.title: What you do
docs.text:
Submit a written progress report to your advisor by June 30:

  • No more than two pages of typed text.
  • Part one: review progress made over the past year.
  • Part two: plans for the future, including prospects for meeting your upcoming deadline.

Who receives it:

Your situation Send the report to Advanced to candidacy Your advisor and all PhD committee members Have an advisor, not yet advanced Your advisor No research advisor yet One of the faculty graduate advisors

Early reports can be brief

It is explicitly recognized that at early stages the report may be little more than a specific account of the past year's activities. As research becomes more focused, the report takes on more the character of an annual report to a contract monitor. Do not agonize over your first one.

docs.title: What comes back
docs.text:
Your advisor's evaluation of the report should contain clear, specific advice. It is documented on a standard evaluation sheet, signed by both the advisor and you.

Your signature only indicates that you have read it — it is not agreement.

docs.title: Exemptions
docs.text:
GEPA exempts two groups from spring evaluations:

  1. Students advancing to candidacy during winter or spring quarter of the current academic year.
  2. Students on an approved leave of absence during spring quarter. In that case the evaluation happens in the first quarter you are registered again.

docs.title: Advisor Reviews
docs.text:
Students' own accounts of what it is like to work with a particular advisor — the information the department cannot publish and prospective students cannot otherwise get.

Read this before you submit

These reviews are not anonymous, and we cannot make them anonymous.

Reviews are submitted through a form and transcribed onto this site by a PGC maintainer, so your GitHub account is never attached to what you wrote. That is the limit of the protection.

  • Faculty can read this wiki. It is public and unrestricted.
  • Details identify people. If an advisor has one student, a review of that advisor identifies its author no matter how it is worded. Small groups, unusual project descriptions, and specific timelines all narrow the field.
  • Removal is not guaranteed. Text removed from a page remains in this repository's git history and is recoverable by anyone who clones it.

Submit at your own discretion. Consider what you are comfortable having attached to you, by inference, permanently.

docs.title: How to submit
docs.text:
1. Fill in the submission form — link to be added by a maintainer.
  2. A PGC maintainer reviews it against the ground rules below and transcribes it onto the advisor's page.
  3. Every entry is dated by the term it was submitted.

You do not edit these pages directly, and you should not — that would put your name on the commit, which is the thing this process exists to avoid.

docs.title: Ground rules
docs.text:
These apply to submitters and to the maintainers who transcribe.

Describe behavior, not character. "Emails typically got a reply in about a week" is useful and checkable. "Doesn't care about students" is neither, and is the kind of statement that creates real exposure for whoever published it. Only your own experience. No second-hand accounts, no "I've heard that." If it did not happen to you, it does not go in. No allegations of misconduct. This page cannot handle those and should not try. Harassment and discrimination go to OPHD; they do not go on a wiki. Nothing about anyone but the advisor. Do not name or describe other students, postdocs, or staff. Date everything. An advisor in 2020 and in 2026 may be very different to work for. A review without a date is worse than no review. Multiple perspectives are the point. Two students can have opposite experiences with the same person and both be telling the truth. Pages hold several accounts; readers weigh them.

docs.title: How to read these
docs.text:
• A single review is one person's experience, not a verdict. Weight accordingly.
  • Check the date. Group culture turns over with its members.
  • Absence means nothing. No page for an advisor means nobody has written one, not that anything is wrong.
  • Nothing replaces talking to their current students. Use this to work out who to approach, not to decide.

docs.title: Page format
docs.text: Each advisor page opens with an at-a-glance table of factual, low-controversy details — group size, meeting cadence, funding pattern, advising style — followed by dated accounts in students' own words.

docs.title: External Fellowships
docs.text:
Fellowships from outside UCSD, split by citizenship requirement. More are listed on the GEPA fellowships page.

Verify before you apply

Amounts, eligibility, and deadlines change every cycle. These entries come from the department's orientation handbook and are a starting point for searching, not an application guide. Always check the program's own site.

Apply early in your program

Several of these are explicitly aimed at students at or near the beginning of doctoral study, and become ineligible after one or two years. If you are a first- or second-year, this is the window.

docs.title: Hertz Graduate Fellowship
docs.text:
Up to $250,000 — cost-of-education allowance plus a personal stipend.

Applicants must be college seniors, first-year graduate students, or in a gap period preparing to apply; intend to pursue a PhD in the applied physical or biological sciences, mathematics, or engineering; intend to direct their studies toward understanding and solving major near-term problems facing society; and be US citizens or permanent residents.

Fannie and John Hertz Foundation · (925) 373-1642 · hertzfoundation.org · fellowshipinfo@hertzfoundation.org

docs.title: SMART Scholarship Program
docs.text:
$30,000–$46,000 stipend depending on degree, plus full tuition and education-related fees and summer internship opportunities.

Requires eligibility to hold a security clearance, participation in summer internships at Department of Defense laboratories, and willingness to accept post-graduate employment with the DoD. Minimum 3.0 cumulative GPA.

Scholarship-for-Service Program · (571) 633-7940 · smartscholarship.org · smart@smartscholarship.com

docs.title: National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate (NDSEG) Fellowship
docs.text:
Full tuition and fees for up to four years, a monthly stipend, and up to $3,600 in medical insurance. No military or service obligation.

For students at or near the beginning of doctoral study in STEM. You must have received or be on track to receive your bachelor's by the end of the academic year, or have completed less than two full-time years of graduate study in the discipline. Requires a research proposal relevant to DoD and at least three recommendation letters.

DoD NDSEG Fellowship Program Office · (301) 948-4232 · NDSEG.PMO@sysplus.com

docs.title: Stewardship Science Graduate Fellowship
docs.text:
$45,000.

For full-time students in disciplines related to high energy density physics, nuclear science, or materials under extreme conditions and hydrodynamics. Summers are spent on full-time research, coursework, or a practicum at a DOE NNSA laboratory. Your department must waive teaching requirements beyond one term.

Krell Institute · (515) 956-3696 · krellinst.org/ssgf

docs.title: Dr. Nancy Foster Scholarship Program
docs.text:
Up to $47,000 — a $35,000 twelve-month stipend plus up to $12,000 education allowance, and up to $10,000 for a 4–6 week collaboration at a NOAA facility. Renewable.

For students pursuing a master's or doctorate in oceanography, maritime archaeology, or marine biology, with a 3.3 GPA or above. Doctoral scholars must complete at least one program collaboration. Women and minority students are particularly encouraged to apply.

NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries · (831) 647-4204 · fosterscholars.noaa.gov · fosterscholars@noaa.gov

docs.title: Amelia Earhart Fellowship
docs.text:
$10,000.

Women of any nationality pursuing a PhD in aerospace-related studies. Full-time, with more than two years of graduate school remaining. Three recommendation letters — one must be from a thesis supervisor or advisor, one from a university professor.

Zonta International · (630) 928-1400 · programs@zonta.org

docs.title: Faculty for the Future
docs.text:
Up to $50,000 for PhD study (up to $40,000 for postdoctoral research). Childcare grants may also be awarded.

For women who are citizens of a developing country or emerging economy, as defined chiefly by the UN Human Development Index. Fellows are expected to return to their home countries after completing their studies to strengthen STEM teaching and research there, or to pursue public-sector positions applying their skills to STEM policy.

faculty4future@slb.com

docs.title: AAUW International Fellowships
docs.text:
$20,000–$50,000.

Open only to women who are not US citizens or permanent residents. Requires the equivalent of a US bachelor's degree by September 30 of the application year, and having already applied to your proposed institution. Applicants must intend to return to their home country after graduation. $30 nonrefundable filing fee. Preference goes to applicants showing prior commitment to the advancement of women and girls.

(202) 785-7700 · aauw@act.org

$500–$10,000, averaging around $3,200.

Open to graduate and undergraduate students studying geophysics or a closely related field, with above-average grades. Two faculty recommendation letters.

docs.title: Funding and Fees
docs.text:
Where the money comes from, what you owe, and what employment covers.

Dollar figures go stale fast

The amounts on this page come from the department's 2025–26 orientation handbook and are recorded to give you a sense of scale. Fees and tuition are reset annually — confirm current figures with the Registrar or the Grad Financial Support Coordinator before relying on them.

docs.title: Assistantships
docs.text:
Graduate students in good academic standing, enrolled full-time (12+ units), may be employed as Teaching Assistants or Graduate Student Researchers up to 50% time — 20 hours per week — during the academic year.

New students admitted with financial support are usually appointed as TAs for one academic year, from the start of fall quarter in September to the end of spring quarter in June.

After the first year, students are encouraged to affiliate with a research group and be supported as a GSR. Ask the faculty member you want to work with well in advance — spring quarter for the following year. GSR funding comes from federal contracts and grants, so it depends on funds being available that year. Some TA positions remain open to advanced students.

Fellowship recipients may also hold part-time TA or GSR appointments.

See Teaching and Research.

docs.title: What employment covers
docs.text:
The 25% rule

Students supported as GSRs or Academic Student Employees (TAs and graders) at 25% time or more during a quarter have their tuition, fees, and health insurance paid for that quarter.

Students awarded TAships or University Fellowships receive full or partial fee and tuition scholarships — the details are in your letter of support. Scholarship payments arrive as an electronic credit on your fee statement once you enroll.

docs.title: If you are not supported
docs.text:

Amount (2025–26) Registration, educational, and health insurance fees $21,375 per year (resident and non-resident) Non-resident tuition, additionally $15,102 per year

docs.text:
US citizens and permanent residents can usually establish California residency after living in the state for one year, which removes the non-resident tuition charge.

To qualify as a resident for tuition purposes you must have established residence in California for more than one year immediately preceding the residence determination date for the term, and have relinquished your previous residence.

Contact the Registrar's Office as soon as you arrive on campus — the clock matters. Details: Residency for tuition purposes.

docs.text:

There are also summer session TA and tutor positions. Direct inquiries to the Student Affairs Manager beginning in April — see Department Directory.

docs.title: UC SHIP
docs.text:
UC SHIP is the student health insurance plan — medical, behavioral health, pharmacy, dental, and vision. It is Affordable Care Act compliant and designed to complement care at Student Health Services on campus.

Enrollment is automatic for registered students. A waiver application is available if you have other coverage.

Waiving has consequences

Students who waive UC SHIP may still use Student Health Services, but modest fees apply to all services, and SHS does not accept or bill other insurance plans. If you waive, look at RAFT (Reduced Access Fee For Tritons), which lets students who waived be seen at SHS for many primary care needs without high costs.

Waiver deadlines and criteria are on the "How to Waive UC SHIP" page. Note the deadline — it is early, and missing it means you are enrolled and billed.

Students employed as TAs, graders, or GSRs at 25% time or more have health insurance covered as a benefit of employment for that quarter — see Funding and Fees.

docs.title: Student Health Services
docs.text:
SHS provides primary medical and urgent care, with laboratory, x-ray, pharmacy, nutrition, and optometry support. Staffed by board-certified primary care physicians and nurse practitioners, some with additional training in reproductive health, sports medicine, urgent care, and mental/behavioral health.

Most services are free for students enrolled in UC SHIP.

Location Library Walk — west of Price Center, south of Geisel Library Hours Monday–Friday, 8:00 a.m. – 4:00 p.m. Phone (858) 534-3300 Fax (858) 534-7545 Email studenthealth@ucsd.edu

Write \"secure:\" in the subject line

When emailing SHS, always begin the subject line with the word secure: to protect your personal information.

Hours change — check the SHS website before making a trip.

docs.title: Pay and Payroll
docs.text:
Getting paid, on time, is mostly a matter of doing three pieces of setup early.

Your first fall paycheck arrives November 1

Quarterly TA salary is split into three equal paychecks. Fall quarter begins in September, but the first check is issued November 1. Plan for roughly six weeks between arriving and being paid.

docs.title: Direct deposit — enroll in all three
docs.text: There are two campus offices handling direct deposit, and domestic students should sign up for all three streams below. You need Single Sign-On for each.

docs.title: 1. Stipend payments — TritonLink
docs.text: Use the TritonLink Direct Deposit tool. Enroll as soon as possible.

docs.title: 2 and 3. Payroll and disbursements — UCPath
docs.text:
Covers payroll (TA and GSR employment checks) and disbursements (travel and other personal reimbursement). Enroll before winter quarter employment.

  1. Log in to UCPath online.
  2. Select Employee Actions → Income and Taxes → Direct Deposit.
  3. Add, update, or delete your direct deposit information.
  4. To add: enter the bank routing number, account type, account number, and the deposit amount or percentage.
  5. Select Save.

Allow two weeks

Initial setup can take up to two weeks to take effect. Enrolling the week before you need money will not work.

UCPath publishes guided simulations for adding, changing, and deleting direct deposit — ask Physics Payroll (hr-ap-phys@ucsd.edu) if you cannot find them.

If you do not enrol, your check is mailed to the home address on your employment paperwork — which is why keeping your address current on TritonLink matters.

docs.title: Employment paperwork
docs.text:
You must complete an I-9 verifying identity and eligibility to work. Bring original documents to orientation: either one document from List A, or one from List B plus one from List C.

List Establishes Examples A Both identity and work eligibility US passport (unexpired or expired) · Permanent Resident Card (I-551) · Certificate of US Citizenship (N-560/N-561) · Certificate of Naturalization (N-550/N-570) · Unexpired foreign passport with I-551 stamp or I-94 showing employment authorization · Employment Authorization Card (I-688A) · Unexpired Employment Authorization Document with photograph (I-688B) B Identity only Driver's license or state ID with photograph · Federal, state, or local government ID with photograph · School ID with photograph · Voter's registration card · US military card or draft record · Military dependent's ID C Work eligibility only Social Security card (unless marked not valid for employment) · Certification of Birth Abroad (FS-545 / DS-1350) · Original or certified birth certificate with official seal · Native American tribal document · US Citizen ID Card (I-197) · Unexpired DHS employment authorization document

The common combination

Most domestic students without a passport bring a driver's license (List B) plus a Social Security card (List C). Bring originals — copies are not accepted.

docs.title: Ecotime
docs.text:
Ecotime is the campus timekeeping system, integrated with UCPath for pay and leave reporting.

Since October 2023, all UAW-represented employees — GSRs, ASEs, postdocs, and some academic researchers — must report time in Ecotime.

Submit a timecard every pay period

You must "Complete" (submit for approval) a timecard each pay period as verification of time worked, even when you have no leave, PTO, or unpaid time to report. A blank period still needs a submitted timecard.

Supervisors and delegates approve timecards on the established schedule. Guidance and office hours are on the Ecotime Blink page.

docs.title: Social Security Number
docs.text:
If you are authorized for paid employment, your employer will request your SSN.

International students need an authorization letter from the International Services and Engagement Office (ISEO) before applying. The full process is on the ISEO Social Security Number page.

Start this early — it gates your ability to be paid.

docs.title: Student Life
docs.text:
Living in San Diego and being a person outside the department.

The official version is elsewhere

Formal services — health, insurance, financial aid, campus offices — are in Resources. This section is for the informal side, which is where a student-run wiki is actually more useful than a handbook.

docs.title: Housing
docs.text:
Grad and family housing is run through HDH. Dormitory accommodation is reserved for undergraduates, so graduate students are looking at campus apartments or the private market.

A variety of rooms and apartments exist within a ten-mile radius of campus. Detailed information comes from the Affiliated Housing Office or HDH Grad and Family Housing.

Apply early

The campus housing queue is long. Get in it as soon as you accept your offer — you can always decline later.

docs.title: What to fill in here
docs.text:
The department's handbook is thin on this, which makes it exactly the gap this wiki should close:

  • Which neighborhoods people actually live in, and rough commute times.
  • Realistic rent ranges — with the date you checked them. Numbers without a date are worse than no numbers.
  • Whether to sign before arriving or find a sublet for a month and look in person.
  • Which listing sites and groups students actually use.

docs.text: Free campus shuttle, the Triton U-Pass for regional transit, and parking options are on Transportation.

docs.title: Community
docs.text: Tea time Graduate students run a weekly tea time during the academic year, with coffee, tea, and cookies. Weekly emails announce the time and location. It is an informal chance to talk physics with faculty, research staff, and other students — and one of the easier ways to meet people outside your cohort. Colloquium PHYS 260, Thursdays at 4:00 p.m. Everyone is expected to attend, and it doubles as a weekly fixed point in the social calendar. PGC The Physics Graduate Council represents graduate students in the department. Reps introduce themselves at orientation. See About PGC. Discord The fastest way to get a question answered — the invite is on the home page. GPSA The campus-wide Graduate and Professional Student Association. Identity and community centers The Cross-Cultural Center, LGBT Resource Center, Women's Center, and others are listed under Campus Services.

docs.title: Cost of living
docs.text:
The September-to-November gap

Your first fall paycheck arrives November 1, but you arrive in September. You need to cover roughly six weeks of rent, deposits, and living costs before any money appears. This is the single most common financial surprise for first-years.

An honest picture of what a stipend covers in San Diego belongs here. Keep it factual, and date every figure.

Keep it general

Do not put individual stipend amounts, offer details, or the finances of named people in this repository — it is public and permanent. General ranges and published pay scales are fine. See About PGC.

docs.title: Campus shuttle — free
docs.text: UCSD students get free, unlimited rides on the Campus Shuttle year-round with their Campus ID card. No pass, no fare, no sign-up.

docs.title: MTS bus and trolley — Triton U-Pass
docs.text:
The Triton U-Pass grants unlimited access to regional MTS and NCTD bus and trolley/light rail routes during the fall, winter, and spring academic quarters.

Note the gap: coverage is by academic quarter, so check what applies over summer if you are here year-round.

docs.title: Parking
docs.text:
Parking permits are available for purchase online.

Don't buy a permit reflexively

If you will not be driving to campus and parking daily, the flexible parking program with ParkMobile is cheaper — you pay per use instead of buying a full permit. Work out your actual number of driving days first.

docs.title: Teaching
docs.text:
Nearly every first-year TAs. This section covers the appointment, the job, and what is expected of you.

It is a degree requirement

Every graduate student must complete at least one quarter of Teaching Assistantship, lecture or lab. Students satisfying it by teaching at UCSD enroll in PHYS 500 in the fall of their first year — mandatory, and only offered in fall. See PhD Requirements.

docs.title: Getting an appointment
docs.text:
If a TA position was part of your support package, you learn your assignment at the department orientation in September, during the TA briefing. There is also a TA application for positions beyond that.

New students admitted with financial support are usually appointed as TAs for one full academic year, from the start of fall quarter in September to the end of spring in June. Appointments run up to 50% time — 20 hours per week — and require full-time enrollment (12+ units) and good academic standing.

You may serve as both a lecture TA and a lab TA over your first year.

International students whose undergraduate degree was not taught in English must certify their English proficiency before they can TA — see English Certification for International TAs. Without it, employment is limited to lower-paying grader positions.

docs.title: The three roles
docs.text: Role What it is Teaching Assistant Preparing and running discussion or lab sections, proctoring, grading, office hours, overseeing graders and proctors, assisting with course administration Grader Mostly grading quizzes and exams, and proctoring Graduate Student Researcher Duties assigned by the faculty member running the funded project

docs.title: Pay
docs.text:
Your first fall paycheck arrives November 1

Quarterly TA salary is split into three equal paychecks. Fall quarter starts in September, but the first check is issued November 1 — roughly six weeks after you arrive. Budget for that gap.

Set up direct deposit immediately, or your check gets mailed to the home address on your employment paperwork. See Pay and Payroll.

Current salary rates are published by GEPA each year; ask the Grad Financial Support and TA Coordinator for the current scale — see the Department Directory.

TAs and GSRs at 25% time or more have tuition, fees, and health insurance covered for that quarter. See Funding and Fees.

docs.title: Reporting your time
docs.text: All UAW-represented employees — GSRs, ASEs, postdocs, some academic researchers — must report time in Ecotime each pay period, even when there is nothing unusual to report. See Pay and Payroll.

docs.title: Training and support
docs.text:
The department partners with the Teaching + Learning Commons, which assigns workshops to help you prepare. A list of available workshops is shared once determined. The Commons also runs a weekly teaching and learning workshop series open to graduate students, postdocs, and faculty, plus a Writing + Critical Expression Hub offering one-on-one writing tutoring, graduate writing retreats, and workshops on graduate-level writing.

Lab TAs for the Physics 1-series get dedicated lab TA training, usually around the day before instruction begins.

docs.title: English Certification for International TAs
docs.text:
All international graduate students must demonstrate oral and aural English competence before being appointed as a TA. This is GEPA policy, established in compliance with the California English Proficiency in Higher Education Act.

This gates your funding

Students whose undergraduate degree was not from an English-speaking institution may not serve as a TA until certified. Failing to certify limits you to lower-paying grader positions. Sort this out before you arrive if you can.

docs.title: Three ways to satisfy it
docs.text: You need one of the following.

docs.title: 1. A qualifying speaking score
docs.text:
Valid at the time of application:

Test Required speaking score TOEFL (Test of English as a Foreign Language) 26–30 IELTS (International English Language Testing System) 8–9 PTE (Pearson Test of English) 84–90

docs.title: 2. Exemption based on a prior degree
docs.text:
If your most recent degree — bachelor's, master's, or doctoral — was earned with a GPA of 3.0 or equivalent (B average) or better from an institution where English is the only medium of instruction, you may already be exempt. This applies to both regionally accredited US institutions and foreign ones.

Verify your institution in the IAU World Higher Education Database (WHED). If English is not listed as the sole language of instruction, no language is listed, or the institution does not appear at all, you must submit exam scores.

WHED is the only accepted proof

No other documentation — letters, language certificates, school websites — can be used in place of WHED to obtain this exemption.

If you received this exemption at admission, you have already met the TA language requirement.

docs.title: 3. Pass the ELCE
docs.text:
Students who have not certified by score or exemption take the English Language Certification Exam, administered by UCSD's English Language Institute.

  • An oral language assessment conducted by a committee.
  • Held before the start of classes — typically between late August and mid-September.
  • You respond to and interact with discipline-specific questions, assessed on vocabulary and comprehensible pronunciation.

The exam date appears on the orientation schedule — see Orientation.

docs.title: Preparation and support
docs.text:
The English Language Program for International Instructors (ELP-II), run by the Teaching + Learning Commons, exists specifically to help international students meet this requirement.

The department also recommends the English Bridge Program for TA training.

docs.title: Lab TA
docs.text: Lab sections run differently from discussion sections, and the training is mandatory.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Lab instruction
  • Answering student questions, in lab and by email
  • Grading lab reports, notebooks, and homework
  • Attending weekly training sessions
  • Maintaining grade records
  • Maintaining a safe lab environment

docs.title: Weekly training sessions
docs.text:
Attendance is not optional

You must attend the weekly training session, where all Lab TAs go through that week's lab with the professor and the Lab TA Coordinator (LTAC). You learn what to cover, what to emphasize, and what problems to expect. If you know you will miss one, tell the LTAC ahead of time.

Physics 1-series lab TAs also get a dedicated training session before instruction begins — see Orientation.

docs.title: How to spend your time in lab
docs.text:
Labs exist so students get firsthand experience and figure things out themselves. Lab TAs are facilitators, not lecturers — your job is to help students find their own solutions.

  • Write your name and email on the board at the start of every lab. Erase what previous sections left behind; ten TA emails on one board is confusing.
  • "Patrol" the lab constantly. Students often have questions they are too afraid to ask. Walk between groups, ask what part of the experiment they are on, ask whether they understand what needs doing, and give them a sense of how they are doing on time.
  • Never sit at the front or back waiting to be asked. If a group has no questions, ask them something that makes them think about why they are doing it. In a mechanics lab: "What would happen if you did this experiment on the moon?"
  • Be patient. A question that seems basic to you is not basic to the student asking it. Part of the job is being available during lab, after lab, and by email.

docs.title: Don't
docs.text:
• Don't use lab computers for games, email, or web browsing.
  • Never work on your own homework or research during a lab session.
  • Don't hang around the lab when you are not teaching.

docs.title: Grading and notebooks
docs.text:
You maintain the student grade records — grade the lab notebooks and enter grades per the professor's instructions.

At the end of the quarter, arrange to return notebooks to students.

Retention rule

Any lab notebook not returned to a student must be retained for one full quarter after the exam period: fall notebooks until the end of winter, winter until the end of spring, spring until the end of fall.

docs.title: Lab safety
docs.text:
Lab TAs and students are expected to wear appropriate personal protective equipment. Closed-toe, closed-heel shoes at all times in the labs.

Know the locations of:

  • The safety shower
  • The eyewash station
  • Fire extinguishers
  • The emergency phone

Emergency numbers are in the Department Directory.

docs.title: Lecture TA
docs.text: What you are responsible for, and how to run a section that actually helps.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
Depending on your instructor's preferences, some or all of:

  • Course material preparation
  • Course website development
  • Occasional lecturing, or attending class meetings
  • Holding discussion and/or problem sessions
  • Supervising and coordinating graders and proctors
  • Using the department's scantron reader to grade scantron exams
  • Preparing homework solutions
  • Coordinating, administering, and proctoring weekly quizzes
  • Coordinating, supervising, and participating in weekly grading
  • Maintaining a complete record of grades
  • Holding weekly office hours

Ask about hours in week one

Preparation load differs enormously between courses. Discuss with your supervising instructor how many hours per week you should be spending on each activity. Do this early, not in week six.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text: Discussion vs. problem sessions The distinction is not always clear. Ask the professor what the purpose and goals of your section actually are. Office hours Make sure the location and times are on the course website and the syllabus. Answering questions You are expected to help students by email in addition to office hours and sections. Check your email at least once a day. Be patient — a question that seems basic to you is not basic to the person asking. Grading You maintain the student grade records. Grade quizzes and enter grades promptly, per the professor's instructions. All grading must take place on campus. Returning work Instructors will tell you how to handle exam papers, scantrons, and homework returns.

docs.title: Running a discussion or problem session
Preparation
docs.text:
• Do all the assigned problems all the way through. Make notes on where students are likely to go off track.
  • Use the same notation, sign conventions, and units as the professor and textbook.
  • Find outside everyday examples and analogies for the current topic.
  • Attend lecture at least once a week so you know where the course is, what notation is in play, and which examples have been used.

docs.title: In the room
docs.text:
• Arrive five minutes early. Write your name, office hours, and email in a corner of the board. Make small talk as students come in — ask how the class is going.
  • Ask for general questions first, then specifics. Write an agenda of what you will cover, and add anything important nobody asked about.
  • Don't try to do too much. Take a vote on what to cut.
  • Look at the students, not the board. Read their faces and interact.
  • Show the physics and the logic, not just the equations. They are learning; they need the steps.
  • Never call something "easy" or "simple." It is easy for you because you are an expert. It is not easy for someone seeing it for the first time.
  • Go light on algebra. If students are struggling mathematically, bring them up to speed at the end of class or in office hours.
  • Avoid lecturing — mix activities. Show demonstrations where possible, and let students play with the demo afterward.
  • Don't burn the session on one question. If it is beyond the course level: "That's a very good question, let's talk about it after class."
  • Don't answer unprepared. If you are unsure, say so and follow up next time or by email. Take every question seriously.
  • Watch your speed. Nervousness makes people talk fast. Move around — it keeps students alert and burns off nervous energy.
  • Never make negative comments about the class, book, or professor. It turns students off the subject.
  • Speak loudly and clearly, and keep everyone involved.
